topics.title: How EBP Began and How It Links to Nursing
topics.summary: Evidence-based practice blends the best current evidence, the nurse’s clinical judgment, and the client’s wishes, and it is now a professional and legal expectation for every nurse.
objectives: You can name the three parts of EBP and what each adds.
You can tell research, evidence, and nursing experience apart.
You can match Nightingale, Cochrane, Sackett, and the IOM reports to their roles, and explain the 17-year gap.
You can link EBP to accountability, the standard of care, health teaching, and QI.
You can apply client choices, cost, and current COPD oxygen care at the bedside.
topics.bigPicture:
At the bedside you will often hear, “This is how we do it here.” Evidence-based practice (EBP) is the habit of asking why. You check whether current evidence supports the practice. Then you fit that evidence to this client, using your judgment.

EBP is why nurses no longer massage red bony areas. It is why we give oxygen to a client with COPD whose oxygen is low. On the NCLEX, EBP shows up as a nurse who cites tradition, a client who refuses care, or a nurse who missed the standard of care. The right answer uses evidence, judgment, and the client’s wishes together.
recap: EBP blends best current evidence, the nurse’s clinical expertise, and the client’s preferences. Honoring an informed refusal is part of EBP.
Research is the process, evidence is the product, experience is judgment, and EBP is the blend.
Nightingale used data to prove sanitation saves lives. Cochrane pushed for randomized trials. Sackett defined evidence-based medicine.
The IOM reports (2001, 2011) made EBP a national quality expectation.
Translational research moves evidence from bench to bedside. The average lag is 17 years.
Champions, teamwork, and education replace tradition without weakening safety.
The standard of care follows the evidence. A retired practice that harms a client can be malpractice.
In COPD, never withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic client. Titrate to about 88–92% and check ABGs.

keyTerms.def: A problem-solving blend of research and evidence with nursing experience. At the bedside: best current evidence, the nurse’s clinical expertise, and the client’s preferences and values.

Clinical decision making that blends three parts (Figure 45.1): the best evidence from current research, the nurse’s clinical expertise, and the patient’s preferences (values, needs, interests, and choices).
A formal, systematic (step-by-step) way of answering a question or approaching a problem.
Nursing knowledge gained from formal, systematic studies or from expert opinion.
The nurse’s steady growth in knowledge, skills, and behaviors that builds clinical judgment.
Using the current best outside (external) evidence plus clinical expertise to make conscientious (careful), explicit (open), and judicious (wise) care decisions. Sackett and colleagues, 1990s.
Turning research findings into real care that improves outcomes (“bench to bedside”). New evidence takes about 17 years, on average, to reach routine use.
Report showing U.S. care caused preventable harm. It urged EBP to reduce unneeded variation and standardize safe care.
Report urging changes in nursing education for better safety, quality, and outcomes through care coordination, health promotion, quality improvement, and EBP.
A person who models a practice change and helps peers replace old habits with evidence-based care.
What a reasonably careful (prudent) nurse with similar training would do in the same situation. Used to judge negligence.
Professional negligence: care falls below accepted standards of practice and causes harm.
An ongoing, data-driven process to improve the why, when, and what of care in one setting.
The client’s right to decide: accept or refuse treatment, seek a second opinion, and make advance directives.
Combining complementary practices, such as mindfulness or acupuncture, with regular medical care in a coordinated, whole-person way.
Choosing care that works while asking if it is available, covered by insurance, and affordable.
An outdated belief that oxygen would stop breathing in clients with COPD who retain carbon dioxide. Hypoxemia means low blood oxygen.

sections.heading: What is evidence-based practice?
sections.keyIdea: EBP is one decision built from three parts: the best evidence, your clinical judgment, and the client’s preferences.
sections.body:
EBP is a way of making decisions, not one fact to memorize. Each decision uses the three inputs below at the same time.

Why all three? Research is done on groups, but your client is one person. Evidence says what usually works. Your assessment says if this client fits. The client says if the plan is acceptable.

Four words get mixed up. Research is the process. Evidence is the product. Experience is the nurse’s growing judgment. EBP is the blend.

Your course guide uses two linked terms. Evidence-based practice is the problem-solving blend of research and evidence with nursing experience. Evidence-based nursing (Figure 45.1) names the three parts you use for each decision. They are the best evidence from the most current research, your clinical expertise, and the patient’s preferences. Preferences reflect the client’s values, needs, interests, and choices.
bullets: Best evidence: What has been shown to work, for whom, and how well?
Clinical expertise: What do my assessment and experience tell me about this client right now?
Client preferences: What does this person value, believe, and choose?
sections.analogy: Think of a three-legged stool: evidence, your judgment, and the client’s values. Take away any leg and the stool falls the moment someone sits on it.

check.q: Research shows early walking prevents complications. A nurse plans to walk a client who just became dizzy and hypotensive. Which EBP leg is missing?
check.a: Clinical expertise (assessment). Stabilize the client first, then mobilize when safe.

sections.heading: Where did EBP come from?
sections.keyIdea: EBP grew from Nightingale’s data, Cochrane’s call for trials, Sackett’s definition, and two national IOM reports.
sections.body:
Florence Nightingale (1850s) was the first nurse theorist and the first nurse to use evidence. In Crimean War hospitals, soldiers in dirty, airless wards died at high rates. She added light, fresh air (ventilation), hygiene, better food, and cleanliness. Infections dropped and more soldiers lived. Her method, shown below, is still the EBP method.

Archie Cochrane criticized how little research backed medical treatments. He urged randomized controlled trials (RCTs). An RCT randomly puts people in a treatment or control group. David Sackett and other clinical epidemiologists then defined evidence-based medicine. The table shows who did what.

Your course guide dates Cochrane’s work to 1971 and says Sackett coined the term “evidence-based medicine.” Most histories date Cochrane’s book to 1972 and credit the term to Gordon Guyatt (1991). Sackett gave the best-known definition. On a course exam, expect 1971 and Sackett. The NCLEX does not test these dates.
steps: Make observations (many deaths in dirty wards).
Collect data (death records).
Analyze the data (deaths cluster with poor sanitation).
Form a hypothesis (sanitation will save lives).
Test it with new data (clean the wards, count deaths again).
Form a conclusion (sanitation lowers death).
Share the process so practice changes.

rows: Crimean War: used observation and death data to prove sanitation saves lives. First nurse theorist and EBP pioneer.
Criticized care with no research behind it; championed RCTs; inspired the international Cochrane Collaboration
Named and defined evidence-based medicine: best external evidence plus clinical expertise, used in a conscientious, explicit, and judicious way
Care had gaps that caused preventable harm; urged EBP to reduce inappropriate variation and standardize safe, quality care
IOM: The Future of Nursing: Leading Change, Advancing Health
Changes in nursing education for safety, quality, and outcomes through care coordination, health promotion, QI, and EBP

check.q: Which step of Nightingale’s method do units most often skip?
check.a: Testing with new data and sharing results. Without outcome data, no one knows if the change helped or harmed.

sections.heading: Why does new evidence take 17 years?
sections.keyIdea: Translational research moves findings from bench to bedside, but the average lag is 17 years.
sections.body:
Translational research turns research findings into real care: “bench to bedside.” The National Institutes of Health (NIH) supports it through the Clinical and Translational Science Awards (CTSA) Consortium.

New evidence takes about 17 years, on average, to become routine care. During that wait, clients get less effective care. Nurses may lack time or skill to read research. Policies and training take time. And tradition is strong: “We’ve always done it that way.”

Any change must improve care without weakening safety or quality. So it is piloted and measured, not forced overnight.
bullets: Tradition: share the evidence, work as a team, and use change agents and respected peers as patient-care champions.
No time, skill, or resources: staff education, journal clubs, and early leader support.
Fear it is unsafe: pilot on one unit and track outcomes.
Surprised clients: teach clients what to expect and why.
sections.example: Nurses hold tube feedings for any residual over 150 mL “because we always have.” A champion shares guidelines: routine holding at low residuals causes underfeeding without reducing aspiration in most adults. The unit pilots a new protocol through the policy committee.

check.q: Staff resist a new bathing protocol: “We’ve always done it this way.” What should the nurse leader do?
check.a: Use peer champions, teach staff the evidence, teach clients what to expect, and pilot the change. Do not force it overnight or dismiss concerns.

sections.heading: How does EBP link to other concepts?
sections.keyIdea: The standard of care is built from evidence, so it changes when the evidence changes.
sections.body:
EBP touches almost every professional concept, as the table shows.

Watch the legal link closely. Courts and boards judge a nurse against the standard of care. That standard is built from clinical knowledge, expert opinion, and research. When evidence changes, the standard changes too. Using a retired practice that harms a client can be malpractice.

Health teaching is another link. Daily habits like sleep, hygiene, and exercise shape future health, so nurses teach self-care backed by evidence.

headers: What it means for the nurse
rows: Best-practice standards, responsibility, and scope of practice reflect EBP.
You are responsible for giving the best, most current care.
EBP gives scientific support to clinical thinking, decisions, and judgment.
As a problem solver, you rely on current best practice in every part of the care plan.
Daily habits (sleep, hygiene, exercise) shape present and future health.
Teach evidence-based self-care that promotes health and lowers illness and injury risk.
Clinical knowledge, expert opinion, and research form professional standards.
Conduct that strays from professional standards is malpractice.
A credible profession has a duty to use EBP.
Blend best evidence with your experience and the client’s preferences.
Improving care is a continuous process that uses current evidence.
Keep improving the why, when, and what of care. This changes how care is delivered.

bullets: Keep the same bed and wake times every day.
Limit caffeine in the afternoon and evening; keep screens out of bed.
Avoid alcohol at bedtime, long naps, and hard exercise right before bed.

check.q: A nurse keeps using a wound method the facility retired because it delays healing. The wound worsens. Which concept is most at issue?
check.a: Legal issues and accountability. The current standard reflects the newer evidence. Falling below it and causing harm can be malpractice.

sections.heading: How do client choices shape the plan?
sections.keyIdea: The client is the third leg: respect informed choices, culture, and cost while still sharing the evidence.
sections.body:
Health beliefs, culture, spirituality, and traditions shape what clients accept. An adult who can make decisions may agree to treatment, such as supplemental oxygen. They may refuse treatment, such as a blood transfusion. They may also seek a second opinion or make advance directives.

Respecting a refusal is not a failure of EBP. It is EBP. Make sure the choice is informed, then offer options the client will accept.

Cost matters too. Ask if the intervention is available and what payment or reimbursement rules apply. Then advocate for cost-conscious, high-value care.

Integrative health combines complementary approaches, such as mindfulness or acupuncture, with conventional care. It stresses interprofessional teamwork and whole-person (holistic) care. In one study of nearly 500 clients with breast or gynecologic cancer, it improved appetite, fatigue, anxiety, pain, sleep, and global health.

rows: Refuses a treatment, such as blood
Confirms understanding, tells the provider, documents, and offers options like blood-conservation strategies
Affirms the right and helps arrange it
Asks what they already use, checks safety (such as herbs with anticoagulants), and coordinates with the team
Asks the case manager and provider about a covered option with similar evidence

sections.example: A client with heart failure says, “I can’t afford a scale, and my family cooks with salted pork.” The nurse finds a free scale through the social worker. She teaches lower-sodium swaps that keep family meals meaningful.

check.q: A client on antiemetics asks if acupuncture could also help her nausea. What is the best response?
check.a: Welcome the question. Explain that some evidence supports it as an addition to, not a replacement for, her antiemetics. Offer to discuss it with the provider.

sections.heading: Box 45.1: Oxygen for clients with COPD
sections.keyIdea: Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic client with COPD; titrate to about 88–92% and monitor ABGs.
sections.body:
This is a classic case of evidence replacing tradition. The old hypoxic drive theory said clients with COPD who retain carbon dioxide (CO2) breathe only because their oxygen is low. Oxygen would “take away the drive” and stop their breathing. So some nurses withheld oxygen, even from very low clients.

Current evidence says hypoxemia itself is the immediate danger. CO2 can rise with uncontrolled, high oxygen. That rise is mostly explained by air-and-blood-flow changes in the lungs and the Haldane effect (oxygen makes hemoglobin release CO2), not a lost “drive.”
steps: Give oxygen when SpO2 is 88% or less. Do not wait for a blood gas.
Titrate (adjust) to about 88–92%, or the range the provider orders.
Check arterial blood gases (ABGs) often for rising PaCO2 and falling pH.
Watch mental status and breathing effort. New sleepiness is a warning sign, so report it promptly.

rows: Give oxygen when SpO2 is 88% or less; hypoxemia is the faster threat
Titrate to a target saturation, not a fixed flow
Also watch ABGs, mental status, and work of breathing

check.q: A client with COPD has SpO2 82%. A colleague says, “Don’t put oxygen on. He’s a CO2 retainer.” What does the nurse do?
check.a: Apply oxygen as ordered, titrate to about 88–92%, and monitor ABGs and mental status. Hypoxemia is the immediate threat.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes in this topic
sections.keyIdea: Most errors mix up tradition, experience, and evidence.
sections.body: Each pair looks alike on a test. The right column tells them apart.

rows: Research creates new knowledge. EBP applies the best existing evidence.
“Studies show…” is evidence. “In my 15 years…” is experience.
EBP is backed by evidence. Tradition is backed by habit.
QI uses local data to improve one setting. EBP brings in outside evidence. They often work together.
Translational applies findings to care. Basic lab research creates new knowledge about disease.
Honoring an informed refusal is EBP. Skipping teaching or alternatives is not.
Cochrane (1970s): randomized trials. Sackett (1990s): defined EBM.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: The best answer uses all three legs: current evidence, assessment, and client involvement.
sections.body:
Items usually show a nurse’s statement or action and ask you to judge it. Common patterns are listed below. Try this sample item.

A senior nurse says, “We always massage red heels and hips. Residents like it.” A new graduate checks current pressure-injury guidelines. Which action best reflects EBP?

A. Keep massaging; the senior nurse’s experience is evidence.
B. Stop massaging red areas, offload and reposition, reassess the skin, and explain why to the resident.
C. Let each resident choose massage or not.
D. Stop all skin care until the unit does its own study.
bullets: “Which statement needs more teaching?” It cites tradition or one expert, or ignores the client.
“Which action best shows EBP?” It blends evidence, assessment, and preference.
Priority items where a safety need, like low oxygen, beats an outdated belief.
steps: Read the stem: a habit conflicts with current guidelines.
What is it really asking? Which option uses all three EBP legs.
Key cues: “always” and “residents like it” signal habit and preference only. Guidelines advise against massaging red bony areas because it can damage stressed tissue.
A is wrong: experience does not override current evidence.
C is wrong: it offers a harmful option without sharing the evidence.
D is wrong: EBP uses existing evidence, and stopping skin care is unsafe.
The answer is B. It applies evidence, reassesses, and involves the resident.

check.q: What reusable strategy does this teach?
check.a: Pick the option that includes evidence, assessment, and client involvement. Options built on one leg alone are distractors.

sections.heading: Worked case: oxygen, a refusal, and a tradition
sections.keyIdea: Treat the physical threat first, then respect the client’s choices and correct the outdated practice through the right channel.
sections.body:
Mr. Okafor, 68, has pneumonia and chronic hypercapnic COPD. His SpO2 is 85% on room air, respirations are 28, and he is anxious. Orders: oxygen to keep SpO2 88–92%, and an ABG in 1 hour.

The night nurse says, “Oxygen will knock out his drive.” Mr. Okafor, a Jehovah’s Witness, says he will refuse blood if his old GI bleed returns.
steps: Recognize cues: low SpO2, fast breathing, and anxiety mean hypoxemia. The handoff reflects the outdated hypoxic drive theory.
Act first on breathing: apply oxygen as ordered and titrate to 88–92%.
Monitor SpO2, breathing, and mental status. Get the ABG. Report drowsiness or rising PaCO2.
Later, share the evidence privately with the night nurse, or with the practice council if the belief is common.
Respect his choice: confirm he understands the risks, tell the provider, document, and offer blood-conservation information.
Evaluate: an hour later, SpO2 is 90%, respirations are 22, and PaCO2 is stable.

check.q: Why did oxygen come before talking with the night nurse?
check.a: Hypoxemia is an immediate breathing threat (ABCs). Peer teaching can safely wait until the client is stable.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In North Carolina, the RN is legally accountable for current, standard-based care, and malpractice is judged against that standard.
sections.body: The NCLEX does not test state laws. These facts explain why NC employers stress current policy and staff education.
bullets: The NC Board of Nursing (NCBON) regulates nursing under the NC Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.).
RN components of practice are in 21 NCAC 36 .0224; LPN components are in .0225.
The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment, based on current standards.
The ANA describes standards, but the state practice act sets the legal scope.
NC malpractice claims generally have a 3-year statute of limitations and a 4-year statute of repose (G.S. 1-15(c)). NC still allows pure contributory negligence as a defense.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state. On a multistate license, follow the laws where the client is.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
bullets: Source: Module 45 study guide, Evidence-Based Practice, outcomes 45.1–45.2, key terms and Sections 2–3, pp. 2759–2761 (Box 45.1 and Focus on Integrative Health).

COPD oxygen: the source says give oxygen at SpO2 88% or less with frequent blood gases. Current guidance (such as GOLD) adds titrating to about 88–92%, or the ordered target, in clients at risk for CO2 retention. Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic client.
Cochrane date: your course guide says 1971. His key book came out in 1972. On a course exam, expect 1971.

Who named EBM: your course guide says Sackett coined “evidence-based medicine.” Most histories credit Gordon Guyatt of McMaster (1991); Sackett gave the widely cited definition (1996). On a course exam, expect Sackett.
The IOM is now the National Academy of Medicine (since 2015). The Future of Nursing 2020–2030 (2021) focuses on health equity.

mnemonics.name: E-C-P stool
mnemonics.text: Evidence + Clinical expertise + Preference = EBP. Missing a leg? It’s not EBP.

mnemonics.name: History in order: “Nurses Can Study In Institutes”
mnemonics.text: Nightingale (1850s data) → Cochrane (1970s RCTs) → Sackett (1990s EBM) → IOM Chasm (2001) → IOM Future of Nursing (2011).

pearls: “We’ve always done it that way” signals tradition. The right answer checks current evidence or policy.
Expert opinion counts as evidence but ranks near the bottom. It does not override strong research.
Respect an informed refusal: inform, explore reasons, notify the provider, document, and offer options.
Hypoxemia kills faster than high CO2. Give oxygen in COPD and titrate to about 88–92%.
Unit-wide change goes through champions, education, pilot tests, and committees. One nurse does not change a policy alone.
redFlags: A colleague withholding oxygen from a hypoxemic client with COPD: treat the client first, then teach.
Forcing treatment on an informed, capable adult violates autonomy and can be battery.
A client replacing chemotherapy or insulin with an unproven product: teach without judging and notify the provider.

checks.q: A strong review shows the unit’s method for checking NG tube placement is unreliable, but policy still requires it. What should the nurse do first?
checks.a: Share the review with the nurse manager or practice council for policy review. Do not act alone or ignore it.

checks.q: A client wants another surgeon to review his scans but fears offending his doctor. What is the best response?
checks.a: Affirm that a second opinion is his right, and offer to help arrange it and get copies of his scans.

checks.q: One nurse cites a famous physician’s opinion. Another cites a large RCT. Which carries more weight?
checks.a: The large RCT. Expert opinion ranks near the bottom of the evidence hierarchy.

checks.q: A client with COPD has SpO2 86%. The ordered target is 88–92%. What does the nurse do?
checks.a: Apply or increase oxygen to reach the target, then monitor SpO2, ABGs, and mental status. Avoid withholding or over-oxygenating.

topics.title: Research Methods, Participants, and Research Ethics
topics.summary: Nursing research uses the scientific method and quantitative or qualitative designs, with informed volunteers protected by IRBs, the Belmont Report, and HIPAA.
objectives: You can put the steps of the scientific method in order and spot a hypothesis.
You can choose a quantitative or qualitative design for a question.
You can explain inclusion and exclusion criteria and name vulnerable groups.
You can describe the nurse’s role in research consent and the right to withdraw.
You can match a situation to respect for persons, beneficence, justice, or HIPAA privacy.
You can say who sets nursing standards nationally and who sets them legally.
topics.bigPicture:
As a new nurse, you may never run a study. But you will care for clients who are in one. A client may say, “I signed up for a study, and I want out.” Knowing research ethics lets you protect that client.

Research methods also help you judge evidence. A study that counts things answers different questions than one that explores feelings. On the NCLEX, this topic shows up as advocacy: a participant who wants to quit, a client pressured to join, or a privacy breach. The right answer protects the client’s rights first.
recap: Nursing research covers practice, education, and administration. Nursing clinical research focuses on client care outcomes.
Scientific method: question, data, hypothesis, study, conclusion.
Quantitative research measures numbers. Qualitative research explores experiences and finds themes.
Participants must meet inclusion criteria, be fully informed, and give consent. Exclusion criteria protect safety and validity.
Research consent is usually written, comes before the study, and can be withdrawn anytime without losing usual care.
The investigator obtains consent. The nurse checks understanding, protects voluntariness, and reports concerns.
IRBs review and monitor studies. Vulnerable groups get extra protection.
Belmont: respect for persons, beneficence, justice. HIPAA protects health information in research.

keyTerms.def: A strict, systematic scientific process to study questions in all areas of nursing: practice, education, and administration.
Research that answers questions to improve client care, such as comparing infection rates or wound care methods.
A step-by-step process: ask a question, collect data, form a hypothesis, run a study, and present a conclusion (Box 45.2).
A testable prediction about how two or more factors are related.
Research that collects numbers through precise measurement and analyzes them with statistics, to summarize and describe findings or to test relationships among variables.
Research that collects words, such as interviews or stories, to explore people’s experiences and find patterns and themes.
Volunteers for a study who meet all the inclusion criteria, have been told about every part of the study, and have given informed consent.
Traits a person must have to join a study, such as age, diagnosis, or disease stage.
Traits that rule a person out of a study, such as pregnancy or certain medicines, often for safety.
The right to learn a study’s purpose, procedures, length, expectations, benefits, and risks before agreeing. Usually written; can be withdrawn anytime.
Pressure, threats, or excessive rewards that make a choice less than voluntary.
Groups who need extra protection in research because their free choice may be limited or they could be exploited.
A child’s or cognitively impaired person’s own agreement to take part, sought in addition to a parent’s or representative’s permission.
A committee that reviews and monitors research before and during a study to protect participants’ rights and welfare.
U.S. report that set three ethical principles for research with people: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.
Researchers know who the participant is but protect that identity and data.
No one, not even the researchers, can link the data to a person.
Federal rule setting national standards that protect identifiable health information, including during research.
Expectations for competent practice. Described nationally by ANA, NLN, and The Joint Commission; defined legally by each state’s Nurse Practice Act.

sections.heading: What is nursing research, and who pays?
sections.keyIdea: Nursing research uses the scientific method: ask a question, collect data, form a hypothesis, test it, and share the conclusion.
sections.body:
Nursing research uses a strict, step-by-step process to study nursing questions in practice, education, and administration. A study of nurse staffing is nursing research. Nursing clinical research focuses on client care, such as comparing two wound dressings.

Every study follows the scientific method (Box 45.2), shown in the steps below. Order matters. A hypothesis before any data is a guess. A conclusion without a study is an opinion.

Research costs money. Grants come from professional chapters and from national and government groups, like those listed below.
steps: Ask a question: Why do more clients here get heel injuries than on the next unit?
Collect data: review skin checks, beds, and turning schedules.
Form a hypothesis: clients who wear heel boots will have fewer heel injuries.
Plan and run the study: give some clients boots and others standard care for 4 weeks.
Present a conclusion: report whether the boots helped, so others can use the results.
bullets: Sigma Theta Tau International (nursing honor society)
Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
National Institute of Nursing Research (NINR)
National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and the American Cancer Society

check.q: A nurse reviews charts and writes, “Clients who walk within 12 hours after surgery will have fewer pneumonias than clients who walk later.” Which step is this?
check.a: A hypothesis: a testable prediction about how two factors (walking time and pneumonia) are related.

sections.heading: Numbers or stories: which design fits?
sections.keyIdea: Quantitative research counts and measures; qualitative research explores what an experience is like.
sections.body:
The question decides the design. Quantitative research asks “how many,” “how much,” or “does X affect Y?” It uses numbers, like pain scores or infection rates, and statistics. The source example compares skin breakdown in infants bathed with water versus soap.

Qualitative research asks “what is it like?” It uses words from interviews, focus groups, or journals. It looks for patterns and themes. The source example explores coping after a radical mastectomy. It helps nurses understand the client’s view.

Neither is better. They answer different questions. Qualitative studies are weaker for proving a treatment works, but they are the right tool for meaning and experience.

rows: How many? Does X affect Y?

sections.example: A nurse interviews 15 clients about why they stopped their heart medicine. Themes of cost and confusion appear: qualitative. Next, she compares readmission rates with and without a pharmacist call: quantitative.

check.q: A study asks parents to describe what helped them cope during their baby’s NICU stay. Which design is it?
check.a: Qualitative. The results will be themes, such as “being included in care,” not statistics.

sections.heading: Who can be in a study?
sections.keyIdea: Participants must meet the criteria, be fully informed, and consent; vulnerable groups get extra protection.
sections.body:
Research participants are volunteers who meet all three conditions: they fit the inclusion criteria, they know every part of the study, and they gave informed consent.

Inclusion criteria say who belongs, such as adults 18–65 with type 2 diabetes. Exclusion criteria rule people out, such as pregnancy or a drug that interacts. Common criteria include age, gender, history, disease stage, and medicines. Criteria protect participants’ safety and keep results valid.

If a participant develops an exclusion condition, like a new pregnancy, hold the study dose and tell the investigator and provider. When you read a study, check if your client resembles the sample.
bullets: Human fetuses and neonates
Children (need parent permission plus the child’s assent when able)
Prisoners (restricted liberty makes pressure easy)
Educationally disadvantaged people
Cognitively impaired people (need a legal representative’s permission plus assent when able)
Pregnant women (special protection under federal rules)

check.q: A prisoner is told he may get an earlier parole hearing if he joins a drug trial. Why is this wrong?
check.a: Prisoners are a vulnerable group. Linking parole to joining is coercion and violates respect for persons. An IRB would not approve it.

sections.heading: Research consent: what does the nurse do?
sections.keyIdea: The investigator explains and obtains consent; the nurse checks understanding, protects the right to withdraw, and speaks up.
sections.body:
Research consent is both legal and ethical. Before agreeing, volunteers must learn the study’s purpose, procedures, length, expectations, benefits, and risks. Consent is usually written and comes before the study starts.

Consent is also ongoing. A participant may ask questions or withdraw at any time. There is no penalty, and usual care continues.

The principal investigator or trained research staff explain the study and obtain consent. The bedside nurse is the advocate. The IRB reviews every study before it starts and monitors it during the study. No study with human participants should start without IRB approval.
steps: Ask the client to explain the study in their own words.
Listen for confusion (“They said I’d be cured”), pressure (“My doctor said I had to”), or wanting out.
If understanding is weak, hold study procedures and ask the investigator to re-explain.
If the client wants out, honor it, notify the research team and provider, and reassure them that care continues.
Document the client’s words and who you notified.

rows: Check understanding and voluntariness, advocate, report concerns
May revoke before or during treatment
May withdraw anytime with no loss of usual care

check.q: Before signing a research consent, a client says, “I don’t really know what this study is, but my doctor wants me in it.” What does the nurse do first?
check.a: Hold the signing and ask the investigator to return and explain. Consent would be neither informed nor voluntary.

sections.heading: Belmont principles and privacy
sections.keyIdea: Respect for persons protects choice, beneficence protects from harm, justice protects fairness, and HIPAA protects health information.
sections.body:
The Belmont Report (1979) came after research abuses such as the Tuskegee syphilis study. The NCLEX will describe a situation and expect you to name the right at risk. The table shows the three principles.

Respect for persons gives extra protection to people with limited (diminished) autonomy. Autonomy can be limited by disability, illness, restricted liberty (such as prison), or immaturity (such as childhood).

Your course guide places strict confidentiality and anonymity under justice. In the original report, justice means fair selection and fair sharing of risks and benefits. Privacy is protected by respect for persons and by federal rules like HIPAA. On a course exam, expect privacy under justice. On the NCLEX, justice items test fair selection.

The HIPAA Privacy Rule sets national standards that protect private health information in research too. Use only the information needed, and store it securely.

Two privacy words get confused. Confidentiality means researchers know who you are but will not tell. Anonymity means no one can tell who you are, like an unsigned survey with no codes. A study that collects names can promise confidentiality, but not anonymity.

rows: Autonomy: voluntary choice with no coercion, full disclosure, and the right to withdraw. Extra protection for people with limited autonomy.
Telling a client their care will suffer if they leave the study
Protection from physical injury, psychological harm, economic loss, and exploitation; the study is done to benefit others
Continuing a study drug after a serious adverse effect
Fair treatment of all participants. Your course also lists strict confidentiality and anonymity here.
Recruiting only free-clinic clients for a risky trial because they are easy to enroll

sections.analogy: Think of a study as a bus trip. Respect for persons is the ticket: you choose to ride and may get off anytime. Beneficence is the seat belt. Justice is the boarding line: no one is pushed on because they had nowhere else to go.

check.q: A research assistant leaves a list of participants’ names and HIV results at the nurses’ station. What does the nurse do first?
check.a: Secure the sheets out of public view, then report the breach per policy. Confidentiality and HIPAA privacy are violated.

sections.heading: What makes nursing a profession?
sections.keyIdea: Research is one mark of a profession, and the state Nurse Practice Act, not the ANA, legally defines your scope.
sections.body:
Nursing is a profession partly because it does ongoing research. The criteria are listed below. The ANA Code of Ethics also requires nurses to protect research participants. So advocacy is a duty, not a favor.

Standards of nursing care come from layers. National groups describe them: the American Nurses Association (ANA), the National League for Nursing (NLN), and The Joint Commission. Legally, each state’s Nurse Practice Act, enforced by the Board of Nursing, defines scope. Facility policy turns both into unit steps.

In a lawsuit, the question is what a reasonably prudent nurse would have done. As research changes guidelines, it changes that answer.
bullets: Specialized education
A well-defined body of knowledge and expertise
Ongoing research
Service to others
A code of ethics
Professional autonomy
Membership in professional organizations

check.q: A new graduate says, “The ANA standards are the law that defines my scope.” Is this correct?
check.a: No. The state Nurse Practice Act, enforced by the Board of Nursing, legally defines scope. ANA standards guide practice but are not law.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes in research
sections.keyIdea: Most errors come from mixing up the two designs, the two criteria, the two privacy words, or the three principles.
sections.body: Each pair looks alike on a test. The right column tells them apart.

rows: Numbers and statistics vs words and themes
Identity known but protected vs identity unknown to everyone
Pressured or not informed vs harmed or exposed to risk
Harm vs unfair selection (“easy to recruit”)
Investigator explains and obtains consent; nurse verifies and advocates
IRB approves and monitors research; ethics committee advises on care dilemmas

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Ask whose right is at stake, then pick the option that protects it now and notifies the right person.
sections.body:
Expect scenarios where a participant’s rights are threatened. Wrong options usually persuade the client to stay, ignore a concern because consent is signed, or breach privacy. Here is a sample item.

A client in a blood pressure drug trial says, “I signed the papers, but I’m scared of side effects and want out. Will I still get treated?” Which response is best?

A. “You signed consent, so you need to finish the study.”
B. “You can withdraw anytime, and your regular care will continue. I’ll tell the research team and your provider.”
C. “Side effects are usually mild. Let’s give it a week.”
D. “I’ll explain the study again so you feel better about staying.”
steps: Read the stem: a participant wants to withdraw and fears losing care.
What is it really asking? The response that is both therapeutic and ethical.
Key cues: “want out” is a withdrawal request; “still get treated” is fear of penalty.
A is wrong: signing consent never removes the right to withdraw.
C is wrong: it minimizes the fear and pressures the client.
D is wrong: re-explaining to keep the client in is persuasion.
The answer is B. It states the right, reassures about care, and notifies the team.

check.q: What reusable strategy fits most research-ethics items?
check.a: Ask, “Whose right is at stake?” Choose the option that honors it and notifies the investigator, provider, or IRB, not one that persuades, delays, or ignores.

sections.heading: Worked case: a child says no
sections.keyIdea: A child’s dissent and comfort come before any research-only procedure, even with a parent’s signed permission.
sections.body:
Maya, 9, is in a mouth-care study for chemotherapy sores. Her mother signed permission. The protocol calls for a mouth swab every 8 hours. At 0200, Maya cries, “I don’t want the swab anymore. It hurts.”

You also see data sheets with participants’ names at the nurses’ station. A new nurse says, “Just do the swab. Her mom signed.”
steps: Recognize cues: Maya is a child, a vulnerable participant. She is refusing (dissent) and reports pain.
Assess her mouth and pain first. Mouth pain needs treatment, study or not.
Hold the research swab. Give comfort and ordered pain medicine.
Notify the research team and provider. Document Maya’s words.
Secure the data sheets and report the privacy breach.
Teach the new nurse: a parent’s signature does not cancel a child’s dissent or the right to withdraw.
Evaluate: pain drops to 3/10, and the team will talk with Maya and her mother in the morning.

check.q: Which Belmont principles were at risk in this case?
check.a: Respect for persons (Maya’s dissent) and justice or confidentiality (the exposed sheets). Beneficence also applies, because her pain came first.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In North Carolina, the Nurse Practice Act sets legal scope, and a minor’s consent law covers treatment, not research.
sections.body: These NC facts support the national rules above.
bullets: Legal scope is set by the NC Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.) and enforced by the NC Board of Nursing (NCBON).
Under 21 NCAC 36 .0224, the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, and evaluation, including reporting when a protocol activity conflicts with a client’s condition.
G.S. 90-21.5 lets minors consent to some treatment: STIs and other reportable diseases; pregnancy (not sterilization or abortion); substance or alcohol use; and emotional disturbance.
That law covers health services, not research. Research with minors follows federal rules and the IRB, which usually require parent permission plus the child’s assent.
NCBON uses a Just Culture approach for practice events, but conduct issues like confidentiality breaches are reported to the Board.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
bullets: Source: Module 45 study guide, Evidence-Based Practice, outcome 45.3, key terms and Section 4, pp. 2762–2763 (Box 45.2, Belmont, vulnerable groups, IRBs, HIPAA, profession criteria, standards).

Belmont justice: your course guide puts strict confidentiality and anonymity under justice. In the original report, justice means fair selection and fair sharing of burdens and benefits; privacy falls under respect for persons and federal rules. On a course exam, expect privacy under justice; NCLEX justice items test fair selection.
Vulnerable groups: federal rules also protect pregnant women, so this was added. Children need parent permission plus their own assent when able.
Consent roles: the source does not say who obtains research consent. This guide teaches the standard rule: the investigator obtains it; the nurse verifies and advocates.

mnemonics.name: R-B-J: “Rights Before Journals”
mnemonics.text: Respect for persons (choice and withdrawal), Beneficence (do good, avoid harm), Justice (fair selection and treatment). Rights come before publishing data.

mnemonics.name: Quan vs Qual
mnemonics.text: Quantitative counts quantities. Qualitative explores the quality of an experience.

pearls: A participant may withdraw anytime, even after signing, with no loss of usual care.
Clinical safety beats the protocol: assess and treat before any research-only step.
Coercion can be subtle: linking joining to better care, privileges, parole, or big payments.
Confidential means “we know but won’t tell.” Anonymous means “no one can tell.”
Use qualitative designs for experience and meaning; quantitative designs for measuring effect.
redFlags: Staff telling a participant they cannot quit: honor the request and notify the investigator.
A client who cannot explain the study: hold study procedures and notify the investigator.
A participant with a serious adverse effect, like black, tarry stools on a study anticoagulant: assess vital signs, notify the provider and research team, and document.

checks.q: A researcher plans to exclude clients taking anticoagulants. What is the most likely reason?
checks.a: Safety, and to keep results valid. Exclusion criteria remove people who could be harmed or who could distort the outcome.

checks.q: A participant asks detailed questions about how randomization works. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Answer basic questions you know, then ask the investigator to give full information. Explaining the protocol in depth is the research team’s job.

checks.q: A survey is returned in sealed envelopes with no names or codes. Confidential or anonymous?
checks.a: Anonymous. No one, including the researchers, can link a response to a person.

checks.q: A man with moderate dementia, enrolled by his daughter, says “no” and pulls away during a study visit. What principle guides the nurse?
checks.a: Respect for persons. Honor his dissent for research-only procedures and notify the investigator.

checks.q: A nurse wants to learn how older adults feel about telehealth visits. Which design fits?
checks.a: Qualitative, because the goal is to explore experience and find themes.

checks.q: Researchers recruit only free-clinic clients for a high-risk trial because they are easy to enroll. Which principle is violated?
checks.a: Justice. It requires fair selection and a fair share of research burdens and benefits.

topics.title: The Four Steps of EBP: One Nurse vs the Whole Unit
topics.summary: EBP has four steps: ask a PICOT question, find the evidence, judge it, then apply, evaluate, and share it, either at one bedside or across an organization.
objectives: You can sort a question as background or foreground, and by type.
You can write a PICOT question and name each part.
You can tell primary from secondary sources and find the parts of an article.
You can judge validity, reliability, and significance, and rank evidence.
You can read a PEP stoplight rating and apply, evaluate, and share a change.
You can tell individual from organizational EBP, and EBP from research and QI.
topics.bigPicture:
This topic is the workflow. It is what you do with a question at 0300, or when your unit wants to fix a problem. The four steps are ask, retrieve, appraise, and apply. They follow the nursing process you already know.

New nurses often slip inside a step. They ask a question too broad to search. They trust a news summary. They confuse “statistically significant” with “worth changing practice.” Or they try to change a policy alone. On the NCLEX, know PICOT parts, the evidence ranking, the stoplight colors, and who can change what.
recap: Four steps: ask a question, retrieve evidence, appraise it, then apply, evaluate outcomes, and disseminate.
Background questions use textbooks and drug guides. Foreground questions use research and PICOT.
PICOT: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome (measurable), Time (optional).
Read primary sources. Article order: title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, conclusion, references.
Appraise validity, reliability, and clinical significance. Statistical significance alone is not enough.
Strongest: large RCTs and meta-analyses. Weakest: personal and expert opinion.
PEP stoplight: green use, yellow not enough evidence, red avoid.
One nurse may adjust own practice within policy. Changing a protocol needs the organizational process.

keyTerms.def: A general “What is…?” question about a disease or drug. Answered with textbooks, medical dictionaries, and drug handbooks.
A narrow, practice-based question about whether an intervention improves outcomes. Answered with research studies.
A format for a foreground question: Population or problem, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, and Time frame (optional). Also called PICO.
Question types: best treatment; accuracy of a test; cause of a condition; likely course and complications over time.
The original article written by the researchers who did the study.
An article in which one author summarizes another author’s original work.
How well a study measured what it meant to measure.
How consistently a study or tool gives the same results each time.
Whether a difference is big and useful enough to change nursing practice.
A math test (often p less than 0.05) showing a result is unlikely due to chance. It does not prove the result matters.
A ranking of evidence strength, from personal opinion (weakest) to large RCTs and meta-analyses (strongest).
Combining the results of many studies on one topic and analyzing them as one large study.
A study that randomly assigns people to a treatment group or a control group. The strongest single design for showing cause and effect.
A study that follows an exposed group and an unexposed group forward over time.
A study that compares people with a condition to people without it, looking back for causes.
Oncology Nursing Society rating: green (strong evidence it works), yellow (not enough evidence), red (strong evidence it fails or harms).
Applying existing best evidence to solve a local problem.

sections.heading: The four steps, starting with the question
sections.keyIdea: EBP runs in four steps that mirror the nursing process, and it starts with a focused foreground question.
sections.body:
Every EBP effort follows the same four steps, shown below. They form a loop, not a line. Results from Step 4 often raise a new question.

Not every question needs research. A background question asks for general facts: “What are the side effects of furosemide?” You answer it with a textbook or drug handbook. New nurses ask many, and that is safe.

A foreground question is narrow: “Does an incentive spirometer, compared with none, shorten a surgical client’s stay?” You answer it with research. Foreground questions drive EBP. They fall into four types, shown in the table.
steps: Step 1, Ask (like assessment and diagnosis): spot a problem and write a PICOT question.
Step 2, Retrieve (like planning): search databases for studies.
Step 3, Appraise (like planning): judge the evidence and rank its strength.
Step 4, Apply, evaluate, and share (like implementation and evaluation).

rows: Which treatment does more good than harm and leads to the best outcomes?
Which test should be chosen, how is it read, and how accurate, safe, and cost-effective is it?
Studies comparing the test to a reference standard
What causes a condition or disease?
What is the likely course over time, and what complications may occur?

check.q: “What is the normal aPTT range for a heparin drip?” Background or foreground?
check.a: Background. It asks for a general fact, answered by a drug reference or protocol.

sections.example: Background questions: “Who is at risk for hypoglycemia?” and “What are the side effects of a specific diuretic?” Foreground questions: “How does using an incentive spirometer, or not using one, affect a surgical client’s length of stay?” and “How does a cooling blanket compare with antipyretic medicine for a client with a high temperature?”

sections.heading: How do you write a PICOT question?
sections.keyIdea: PICOT turns a vague worry into a searchable question; the outcome must be measurable.
sections.body:
PICOT gives a foreground question five parts. The table walks through an example. Time is optional, but it helps.

Three errors are common. The outcome cannot be measured, like “feel better.” The comparison is missing, so there is nothing to test against. Or the intervention and outcome are swapped. Words like “reduce” or “rate of” usually mark the outcome.

rows: P: Population or problem of interest
Shared traits of the client group: age, gender, health problem
I: Intervention (or prognostic factor or exposure)
What will be done: a treatment, medicine, therapy, or new care routine
Incentive spirometer 10 times an hour while awake
The control or main alternative: standard care, placebo, no intervention, or a different intervention
Deep breathing and coughing without a spirometer
The desired, measurable effect, such as symptom relief, fewer procedural errors, or higher satisfaction
How long the study runs, or the time to reach or measure the outcome, such as 12 hours, 4 weeks, or 6 months

sections.example: Brent, a nurse educator, sees IV pump errors among new nurses. His question: “In new med-surg nurses (P), does simulation training (I) compared with lectures (C) reduce pump errors (O) over 6 months (T)?”

check.q: “For adults with dementia, does music therapy compared with usual activities reduce agitation over 4 weeks?” What is the C?
check.a: Usual activities. Music therapy is the I, less agitation is the O, and 4 weeks is the T.

sections.heading: Step 2: Where do you find evidence?
sections.keyIdea: Go to the primary source in a trusted database; a news story or sales brochure is not enough.
sections.body:
A primary source is the original article by the researchers. A secondary source is someone else’s summary, like a news story, and can get details wrong. A review-of-literature article presents many studies and ends with a recommendation. When it matters, read the primary source.

Search trusted databases, listed below, not social media. Articles follow the order in the table. The abstract shows relevance. The methods show how far to trust it.
bullets: CINAHL: the core nursing database (through EBSCO)
PubMed/MEDLINE: biomedical research
Cochrane Database: systematic reviews
EBSCO tools such as DynaMed and PsycINFO
ScienceDirect (Elsevier), AHRQ, Evidence-Based Nursing (BMJ), and the Fuld Institute for EBP

rows: A short summary of the whole article
The question or focus, plus older research on the same hypothesis
Interprets the results against the hypothesis and evaluates the findings

check.q: A nurse wants to know how many people were in a study, how they were chosen, and what tool measured the outcome. Which section?
check.a: Methods.

sections.heading: Step 3: Can you trust the study?
sections.keyIdea: Check validity, reliability, and clinical significance; a tiny difference can be statistically significant yet not worth changing care.
sections.body:
Validity asks: did the study measure what it meant to? Counting call-light presses to measure pain is weak, because call lights mean many things.

Reliability asks: are results consistent? A pain tool that gives two nurses very different scores for the same client is unreliable.

Clinical significance asks: is the difference big enough to change care? Statistical significance, often p less than 0.05, only means the result is unlikely to be chance. A real but tiny benefit may not justify more cost or nursing time.
sections.analogy: Think of a bathroom scale. If it reads 150 when you weigh 170, it is not valid. If it reads 150, then 162, then 141, it is not reliable. If it reads 150 every time when you weigh 170, it is reliable but still not valid. A 0.2-pound drop may be real, but it is not clinically significant.

check.q: A large study finds a new protocol lowers pain from 5.2 to 4.8 (p less than 0.01), but it adds 20 minutes of nursing time per client each shift. What should the nurse conclude?
check.a: It is statistically significant but may not be clinically significant. The small benefit may not justify the extra time.

sections.heading: How strong is the evidence?
sections.keyIdea: Large RCTs and meta-analyses sit at the top, opinions sit at the bottom, and the PEP stoplight turns evidence into go, caution, or stop.
sections.body:
The hierarchy (Figure 45.3) ranks evidence from weakest to strongest, as the table shows. RCTs rank high because random assignment spreads hidden differences evenly. The control group gets no intervention, and the experimental group gets it. So a difference in outcome can be credited to the treatment. A meta-analysis combines many studies and analyzes them as one large study.

Some designs only observe. A cohort study is longitudinal: it follows an exposed group and an unexposed group forward over time. A case-control study compares people with and without a condition to find predictive factors (variables). Both suit etiology and prognosis but cannot prove cause like an RCT. A case study describes one person, issue, or event.

The Oncology Nursing Society’s Putting Evidence into Practice (PEP) uses a stoplight, listed below.

rows: Interviews about living with heart failure
Fall rates before and after rounding, no randomization
Large RCTs and meta-analyses of controlled studies

bullets: Green: strong evidence it is likely effective. Use it.
Yellow: not enough evidence to know if it helps or harms. Use caution and involve the provider.
Red: strong evidence it is likely ineffective or harmful. Avoid it and teach why.

check.q: Researchers find 200 nursing-home residents with pressure injuries and 200 without, then compare past nutrition. Which design is this?
check.a: Case-control. It starts with the condition and looks back for causes.

sections.heading: Step 4: Apply it, at bedside or unit-wide
sections.keyIdea: Apply the evidence with judgment and preference, measure results, then accept, reject, or modify; changing a protocol needs the organization.
sections.body:
Step 4 blends the best evidence with your assessment and the client’s wishes. Then you watch results and share them. Sharing, or dissemination, closes the “EBP loop.”

Who can make the change? An individual nurse can adjust their own routines right away, within scope and current policy, like using teach-back. An organizational change affects a protocol, product, policy, or form. It needs the process in the table.

Do not mix up three activities. A research study creates new, general knowledge under IRB oversight. An EBP project applies existing evidence to a local problem. Quality improvement uses local data and quick cycles, like Plan-Do-Study-Act.
steps: Blend the evidence with assessment findings and client preferences.
Carry out the change for one client, or on a pilot unit.
Check fidelity: is it being done the way the evidence describes?
Measure intended outcomes and watch for unexpected ones.
Decide: accept, reject, or modify, based on the data.
Share results informally on the unit or in the agency, or formally at national conferences and in professional nursing journals.

rows: Specific questions about the clients assigned to this nurse
Division- or hospital-wide protocols, policies, and procedures that affect large groups of clients
Nurse evaluates and adjusts own routines, within scope and facility policy
Leadership approval, interprofessional committee, stakeholder buy-in, formal policy and procedure revision
Right away, at the bedside, to improve outcomes such as shorter stays or higher satisfaction
Staff champions, continuing education, pilot tests, ongoing quality and safety audits

check.q: After a new oral-care protocol, pneumonia falls but clients report more mouth soreness. What should the team do?
check.a: Evaluate the unexpected effect and likely modify the protocol, such as a different product. Evaluation covers both intended and unintended results.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes in the steps
sections.keyIdea: Most errors swap PICOT parts, misrank evidence, confuse the two kinds of significance, or act alone on a unit-wide change.
sections.body: Each pair looks alike on a test. The right column tells them apart.

rows: “What is…?” vs “Does X compared with Y improve…?”
The new thing tried vs standard care, placebo, or usual care
Written by the researchers vs someone’s summary
Measures the right thing vs gives the same result each time
Unlikely due to chance vs big enough to change care
Follows groups forward vs starts with the condition and looks back
Not enough evidence vs strong evidence of no benefit or harm
Applies existing evidence locally vs creates new knowledge with an IRB
Own practice within policy vs any change to a unit protocol, product, or form

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Place the scenario on the four-step map and choose the very next step, never a skipped one.
sections.body:
Items ask you to name a PICOT part, rank evidence, act on a rating, pick the next step, or choose the right channel for change. Distractors skip a step or misrank evidence. Here is a sample item.

A nurse reads a newspaper story about another hospital’s new skin-prep routine that cut surgical infections. She wants her unit to adopt it. What should she do next?

A. Start using it for her own clients tomorrow.
B. Find and appraise the original study and related research before proposing a change.
C. Ask the surgeons which routine they prefer.
D. Write a new unit policy and post it.
steps: Read the stem: a secondary source (newspaper) and a unit-wide goal.
What is it really asking? The next step in the EBP process.
Key cues: nothing has been retrieved or appraised yet.
A is wrong: it skips Steps 2 and 3 and goes outside policy.
C is wrong: preference is opinion, the weakest evidence.
D is wrong: one nurse cannot write unit policy.
The answer is B. Retrieve and appraise before any proposal.

check.q: What reusable strategy fits “next step” items?
check.a: Find where the nurse is on the four-step map. Pick the very next step. Reject options that jump ahead or skip the organizational process.

sections.heading: Worked case: fewer catheter infections on 6 West
sections.keyIdea: A unit-wide change runs through all four steps and the organization’s approval, then gets measured and adjusted.
sections.body: You are a staff nurse on a 32-bed medical-surgical unit. Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) are twice the hospital benchmark. Catheters often stay in for days after they are needed, because removal needs a provider order. Your manager asks you to join a team.
steps: Ask: “In adults with urinary catheters (P), does a nurse-driven removal protocol (I) compared with removal by provider order (C) reduce CAUTIs (O) over 6 months (T)?” It is a therapy question.
Retrieve: search CINAHL, PubMed, and Cochrane for primary studies and reviews.
Appraise: a meta-analysis and several before-and-after studies show fewer catheter days and CAUTIs. Check validity, reliability, and clinical significance.

Go through the organization: take the evidence to the manager and practice council. Build a team: leaders, an educator, frontline nurses, the manager, a QI specialist, infection prevention, and providers.
Apply: pilot the approved protocol with peer champions, and teach clients why catheters may come out sooner.
Evaluate: CAUTIs fall 45%, but reinsertions rise slightly in orthopedic clients. The team modifies the bladder-scan threshold for them.
Share: present at nursing grand rounds and submit a conference poster.

check.q: Why couldn’t nurses just start removing catheters without orders after reading the evidence?
check.a: Removing a catheter without an order or approved protocol is outside policy. Organizational change needs approval and a formal protocol first.

sections.heading: Worked case: Brent Calloway’s simulation project
sections.keyIdea: An EBP project applies existing evidence to a local problem; the right team makes the change relevant, accepted, and lasting.
sections.body: Brent Calloway is a nurse educator. New medical-surgical nurses are making procedural errors, such as IV pump mistakes. Studies already show that simulation-based competency training reduces these errors. Brent wants to bring that training to his units. Follow his project in four parts.
steps: Part 1, the question: “In new med-surg nurses (P), does simulation-based competency training (I) compared with lectures (C) reduce procedural errors (O) over 6 months (T)?” This is a therapy question.

Part 2, research or EBP project? A peer asks if Brent is doing a research study. He is not. Research creates new knowledge that applies widely (generalizable knowledge), using strict controls. Brent is translating existing best evidence into practice to fix one unit problem. That is an EBP project.

Part 3, the team: a vice president (leadership), staff development educators, frontline med-surg nurses, a nurse manager, and a quality improvement specialist. Why: frontline nurses keep it clinically relevant and win unit buy-in. Leaders approve it. The QI specialist measures it. Together they make the policy change last.

Part 4, roll it out: this is an organizational change. It needs leadership approval and a revised competency policy. Roll it out with champions, education, and a pilot. Track error rates and audits. Accept, reject, or modify the program. Then share the results.

check.q: Brent’s manager suggests leaving frontline nurses off the team “to save time.” What is the best reply?
check.a: Frontline nurses do the procedures. They keep the change clinically relevant and build unit buy-in. Without them, the change is less likely to last.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In North Carolina, a protocol supports RN judgment but never replaces it, and the RN delegates tasks, not judgment.
sections.body: These NC rules shape how a new protocol is carried out.
bullets: Under the NC Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A) and 21 NCAC 36 .0224, the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment.
With a new protocol, the RN still assesses and evaluates each client.
The RN may delegate protocol tasks, such as a Nurse Aide I recording urine output, but not judgment, such as deciding a catheter meets removal criteria.
The task must be on the aide’s approved list, and the RN must judge it right for this client. NA I registry: NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation. NA II registry: NCBON.
NCBON publishes a Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP and a scope-of-practice decision tree.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
bullets: Source: Module 45 study guide, Evidence-Based Practice, outcomes 45.4–45.5, Sections 5–6, pp. 2763–2768 (Tables 45.1–45.4, Figure 45.3, PEP stoplight, Brent Calloway case).

Hierarchy: most current models (such as Melnyk and Fineout-Overholt) put meta-analyses of RCTs at the top and single RCTs just below. The guide teaches that a meta-analysis of RCTs is the strongest evidence and an RCT is the strongest single design. This fits the source.
Statistical significance and QI (including Plan-Do-Study-Act) were added because NCLEX items often contrast them.
PEP yellow is taught as: not enough evidence to know if it helps or harms.
The stoplight is simplified. ONS uses more detailed categories, from “recommended for practice” to “not recommended for practice,” that group into the three colors.

Brent Calloway case: the course guide gives two takeaways from Parts 1–4 (EBP project vs research study, and team selection). This guide lays out all four parts as steps; the PICOT and rollout details follow the guide’s Section 5–6 content.

mnemonics.name: A-R-E-A: the four steps
mnemonics.text: Ask (PICOT) → Retrieve → Evaluate → Apply (then evaluate outcomes and share). “Work in your AREA.”

mnemonics.name: Stoplight
mnemonics.text: Green = go. Yellow = caution, not enough evidence. Red = stop, it fails or harms.

pearls: In PICOT, C is often standard or usual care, and O must be measurable.
Meta-analyses of RCTs and large RCTs are strongest; personal and expert opinion are weakest.
After a change, look for unexpected effects, then accept, reject, or modify.
A strong team includes a staff development educator, a QI specialist, the nurse manager, and frontline nurses.
redFlags: Changing practice based on one unappraised article or a sales brochure.
Using a red-rated intervention without talking with the client and provider.
Skipping outcome checks after a change, so harms go unseen.
Following a protocol step when the client is unsafe, such as walking a client whose blood pressure dropped: stop, sit them down, and reassess.
Delegating a protocol decision that needs judgment, such as whether a catheter meets removal criteria, to an aide.

checks.q: A client asks if an herbal tea will help her cancer fatigue. PEP rates it yellow. What does the nurse say?
checks.a: “There isn’t enough evidence yet to know if it helps or harms. Let’s ask your provider.”

checks.q: A new graduate reads a strong CLABSI meta-analysis. Policy requires a daily chlorhexidine bath. Which change can she make on her own?
checks.a: Give the required daily bath at a time the client prefers. Changing the dressing or flush routine would need the organizational process.

checks.q: An educator applies proven simulation training to reduce pump errors. Is this research?
checks.a: No. It is an EBP project, because it applies existing evidence to a local problem.

checks.q: Three months into a sepsis protocol, antibiotics are faster but unneeded blood cultures have risen. What should the team do?
checks.a: Keep monitoring both outcomes, review where the protocol is misapplied, and modify the protocol or staff education.

checks.q: Under an approved catheter-removal protocol, which task can the RN delegate to a Nurse Aide I?
checks.a: Measuring and recording each voided volume. Deciding if the client meets removal criteria stays with the RN.
